articles.title: CURTIS HILL: DEI is bad for the Black community. Merit is key for Black achievement
articles.summary: Stephen A. Smith told Trump that the DEI rollback is scaring corporations away from supporting HBCUs, and the president said he would look into it.
articles.body: Stephen A. Smith sat down with President Donald Trump at the White House in mid-October and made a point that deserves more attention than the usual partisan scorekeeping. The ESPN commentator told Trump that the aggressive rollback of DEI programs has produced an unintended side effect: Private corporations are growing hesitant to support historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs). Donors fear that a gift once viewed as ordinary philanthropy will now be read as a DEI initiative, inviting government scrutiny or accusations of engaging in racial preferences. Smith, an HBCU graduate, said the president acknowledged he had not fully considered that chilling effect and said he would look into it. The conversation was useful precisely because it separated opposition to race-based mandates from hostility toward Black institutions and people. STEPHEN A SMITH DOUBLES DOWN ON TRUMP DINNER, CHALLENGES CRITICS BY ASKING, 'WHAT THE F--- ARE YOU DOING?' That distinction is essential. Opposition to DEI programs that impose racial quotas, "check-the-box" hiring or the elevation of identity over competence is not anti-Black. It is pro-equality and pro-merit. Preferential treatment that sorts Americans by race, ethnicity or sex violates the principle of equal treatment and, in some circumstances, runs afoul of federal anti-discrimination law. It substitutes political fashion for individual achievement. OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE CLEARS WAY FOR WHITE EMPLOYEE TO CHALLENGE SEATTLE'S DEI POLICIES Companies and universities that adopted these systems after 2020 often did so under intense social and reputational pressure, not because rigorous analysis showed they improved performance or expanded genuine opportunity. Corporate shareholder proposals seeking disclosure of the actual return on DEI spending — including net present value, litigation risk and opportunity costs — have been necessary correctives. They do not attack Black Americans. They challenge a management ideology that treats race as a proxy for qualification. The danger arises when the correction overshoots. MEDICAL SCHOOLS ACCUSED OF REBRANDING DEI PROGRAMS TO EVADE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SCRUTINY When federal agencies, corporations and advocacy groups begin treating almost any race-conscious activity as suspect or potentially illegal, rational actors respond by avoiding the perceived risk altogether. Federal agencies have terminated or paused some research awards and outreach efforts involving HBCUs and other minority-serving institutions after determining that they conflicted with administration priorities or anti-DEI directives. Private foundations and corporate philanthropy have followed a similar pattern of retreat. STEPHEN A SMITH DEFENDS WHITE HOUSE DINNER WITH TRUMP The practical result risks becoming a de facto hands-off policy toward Black institutions, even when the stated motive is colorblindness or risk avoidance. That outcome serves no one who believes in free markets and equal opportunity. Black Americans, like every other group, benefit when talent, capital and institutions can connect without artificial barriers or artificial preferences. HBCUs have long played an outsized role in educating Black professionals and creating pathways into engineering, medicine, education, business and other fields. Voluntary corporate support for those institutions — for skills training, small-business capital or rigorous recruiting — is not the same thing as mandatory racial quotas in a corporate boardroom or university admissions office. One expands the pool of qualified competitors; the other distorts the competition once that pool exists. ELI STEELE: CALIFORNIA FORCES COMPANIES TO MINE THE PAST FOR SLAVERY'S SINS Conservatives and free-market advocates who oppose DEI must make this distinction clear. When federal agencies, corporations and advocacy groups begin treating almost any race-conscious activity as suspect or potentially illegal, rational actors respond by avoiding the perceived risk altogether. Silence or indifference to the chilling effect invites the accusation that the real goal is exclusion rather than fairness. Critics will make that charge regardless; conservatives should give them no ammunition. The constitutional and economic case against race preferences is strongest when paired with a clear commitment to expanding access: better K-12 preparation, vocational pathways, capital formation and the removal of unnecessary licensing and regulatory barriers that limit entry for everyone. Merit is not the enemy of Black advancement. It is the only durable basis for it. Industry, competence and character should be rewarded wherever they appear. Bigotry should be excluded by ordinary business judgment and by law, not by new forms of discrimination that simply reverse the old ones. Smith’s observation is a reminder that policy has second-order effects. Rejecting the check-the-box games of DEI does not require abandoning engagement with Black institutions or individuals who compete on the merits. It requires the opposite: confidence that free enterprise, equal rules and voluntary association will produce more durable opportunity than either racial set-asides or fear-based withdrawal. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The goal should be neither a system that rewards mediocrity in the name of equity nor one that treats Black Americans as too risky to include. It should be a system that expands the field of competition and then judges the results without regard to ancestry. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That standard is both constitutional and practical. It is also the only one that treats Black Americans as full participants rather than permanent subjects of a political project. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM CURTIS HILL

articles.title: What’s the Falklands oil project at the heart of latest UK-Argentina spat?
articles.summary: UK says it will defend its interests at tribunal hearing, as Argentina seeks measures to block the offshore project.
articles.body:
The United Kingdom has pledged to defend its interests in the Sea Lion project to develop an oilfield near the Falkland Islands, as Argentina has brought a legal challenge before a tribunal over the offshore oil exploration, citing environmental concerns.

Attorney General Ellie Reeves, representing the UK government at the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS), said billions of pounds that are crucial to the future of the Falkland Islands will be lost if Argentina is successful in getting the project blocked.

The Hamburg-based tribunal is sitting for two days as Argentina seeks a provisional ruling to suspend oil drilling.

Reeves also said Argentina’s objection to the development was rooted in its territorial claims. “The hearing is not about the sovereignty of the Falklands,” the UK prime minister’s official spokesman said on Monday, echoing his country’s position that the island’s sovereignty is not up for negotiation.

The dispute is the latest in rising tensions between the UK and Argentina over the British overseas territory in the South Atlantic Ocean.

The Sea Lion development is a UK-Israeli venture to drill for oil in waters administered by the Falklands.

The UK’s Rockhopper Exploration and Israel’s Navitas Petroleum, operator of the Sea Lion oilfield, located about 220km (137 miles) from the islands, are expected to start the project in March 2027, with oil production to begin in 2028.

According to Rockhopper Exploration, the Sea Lion exploration field holds an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil in place, of which 500 million barrels are recoverable resources.

However, Argentina’s President Javier Milei announced measures to block the development in September and said in a post on X that he had instructed the Foreign Ministry and the country’s legal teams to initiate arbitration proceedings against the UK.

“If in 2 weeks the United Kingdom does not halt the illegitimate exploitation, we will go to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea. THE MALVINAS ARE ARGENTINA’s, and they are defended with facts, not words,” he wrote, using the Argentinian name for the Falkland Islands.

Argentina formally filed a complaint at the tribunal seeking provisional measures against the UK on October 13.

The UK has administered the Falkland Islands since 1833. However, as the territory lies off Argentina’s shores, Buenos Aires claims sovereignty over what it calls Las Malvinas.

Milei has also threatened tougher sanctions on companies involved in the oil exploration project, preventing them from operating in Argentina’s oil and mining sectors.

Milei’s government argues the project violates a United Nations resolution calling on both sides to refrain from unilateral actions in the islands until their dispute over the territory’s sovereignty is resolved.

But Jorge Emilio Nunez, a reader in legal philosophy at Manchester Metropolitan University, explained that at the core of the proceedings lies the sovereignty question over the Falklands.

“The oil project is the current trigger, but it sits on top of deeper competing claims about title, the self-determination of the islanders, and control of the surrounding maritime spaces and resources,” Nunez told Al Jazeera.

“This is not only a legal dispute. It also involves domestic politics and leaders’ prestige on both sides. When valuable natural resources become commercially viable, the underlying territorial disagreement is reactivated and reframed through legal, environmental and economic arguments. The resource issue does not replace the sovereignty dispute; it intensifies it.”

On Tuesday, Reeves told the Law of the Sea Tribunal, which issues legally binding rulings on maritime disputes, that Argentina wanted to “take control of those resources for itself”.

“The provisional measures sought by Argentina would prevent the people of the Falkland Islands from developing their natural resources as they are entitled to do so, pursuant to their fundamental right to self-determination,” she said, according to The Guardian.

“The measures sought would have devastating consequences for the Falklands people. They risk losing billions of pounds in money, which is essential for the islands’ economic development.”

But Argentina’s lawyer, Mario Oyarzabal, argued that action was needed to block the project.

“[Argentina] respects the interests of the inhabitants of the islands and their way of life as enshrined in the Argentine constitution…What these British citizens do not have is a right to decide to which state the islands belong,” he said during the hearing, The Guardian reported.

“These resources belong to the Argentine people. Some 46 million of them, including the 1,247 inhabitants born on the islands, whose interests will be duly taken into account,” he added.

In 2013, Falkland islanders voted overwhelmingly to remain with the United Kingdom, despite Argentina’s claims.

On Monday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s official spokesperson told the Independent news outlet that the UK was “fully engaged in the UNCLOS [UN Convention on the Law of the Sea] process, and we’ll clearly set out our position on Argentina’s request for provisional measures before the Tribunal”.

“We’ll continue to robustly defend our interests and those of the Falkland Islanders,” the spokesperson added.

Last month, Burnham also discussed the bid to block the oil project during a call with United States President Donald Trump .

“The prime minister raised the economic consequences of Argentina’s coercive measures for the UK and US and reiterated the importance of respecting the islanders’ right to develop their natural resources,” Burnham’s office said.

The fraught relationship between the UK and Argentina remains tense and heavily focused on the Falkland Islands.

Milei has capitalised on Trump’s refusal to say whether Washington would support the UK in a future conflict over the Falklands after the US president criticised London for not doing more to support the US during its attacks on Iran.

In September, Milei said the “winds of change” were blowing in Argentina’s favour when it comes to its claims of sovereignty.

“The United States is considering this change in position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with Western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come,” Milei said.

At the same time, Argentina is set for an election next year, when the Sea Lion project’s halt could help Milei’s polling position.

To Nunez, the tribunal could have a “modest domestic impact” in the country.

“A visible legal success would allow the government to claim it is actively defending national interests and resources as the Falklands/Malvinas issue carries strong symbolic weight (the slogan “Las Malvinas son Argentinas” is still, intentionally, heavily used),” he said.

However, he noted, “A setback could be used by opponents”.

“Overall, while the case will be used for political messaging in Argentina, Argentine voters tend to prioritise economic performance over developments in the sovereignty dispute.”

articles.title: A blue wave could not stop trans athlete bans
articles.summary: Advocates for transgender Americans are trying to pick up the pieces and move forward after suffering significant defeats at the ballot box even amid last week’s historic blue wave. Arizona, Nebraska, Washington and Colorado all passed measures seeking to bar transgender women and girls from female sports teams, showing troubles for trans rights even…
articles.body:
Advocates for transgender Americans are trying to pick up the pieces and move forward after suffering significant defeats at the ballot box even amid last week’s historic blue wave.

Arizona, Nebraska, Washington and Colorado all passed measures seeking to bar transgender women and girls from female sports teams, showing troubles for trans rights even in Democratic strongholds.

Supporters of transgender athletes are planning education campaigns and say there is much work to be done to lay the groundwork for upcoming battles.

“I certainly don’t think the fight is over for trans kids in sports, but I do think this election made it pretty clear that people have a long way to go before they understand what it means to support transgender rights, and that includes ability to play in sports,” said Shelby Chestnut, executive director of the Transgender Law Center.

The four statewide measures that passed last week created or expanded restrictions on transgender athletes at either the K-12 or college level, and polls show the public largely remains behind such measures.

The Research Institute at Siena University in April found that 59 percent of those surveyed opposed transgender athletes competing at the high school level on teams that align with their gender identity, while 58 percent felt the same about college athletes.

Those numbers were down from 2025, when Siena University found 65 percent were opposed to transgender athletes competing on their preferred teams at the high school and college level.

Trans rights activists were encouraged that some of the ballot measures passed by narrow margins — Colorado’s cleared with 52 percent — saying the results, while disappointing, show progress is being made.

“Within a remarkably short period of time, I mean, under the pressure of having these measures on state ballots, we were able to shift public opinion really dramatically,” said Shannon Minter, legal director at the National Center for LGBTQ Rights.

The ballot measures themselves were a new tactic for those aiming to place restrictions on transgender athletes. Twenty-seven states have enacted laws against trans athletes — and two others are doing so through regulations — but putting the issue directly in front of voters is a shift, and a successful one for opponents.

“I think it was genius, and it was a great way to be able to protect girls sports,” said Beth Parlato, senior legal counsel at the Independent Women’s Forum.

Parlato said while she hopes to see this strategy adopted in more states, the ultimate goal would be legislation “passed nationally” on the issue.

Advocates for transgender athletes argue it is a battle they can win with more time. Less than 1 percent of American athletes are estimated to be transgender, and supporters say the issue should be dealt with locally.

“When the public does have a chance to understand that … we’re not talking about an all-or-nothing issue, that there can be reasonable rules that we can look at the age of the kid, the sport, the level of competition. People are supportive because people generally don’t want to exclude anybody,” Minter said.

“The other realization that people begin to have, and I think is another reason these votes were so close, is people begin to realize that the primary effect of measures like this is to actually subject all girls to a level of scrutiny and potentially very invasive examinations or testing that is just really off-putting to most people,” Minter added.

Brian K. Bond, the CEO of PFLAG, an LGBTQ advocacy group, said it is important for people to build relationships and have “difficult conversations” to advocate for transgender people.

“That means reaching beyond our usual circles and getting outside the bubbles created by our algorithms,” he added.

The movement will also be looking at litigation and pressure on elected officials as part of the campaign to push back.

“I know that some groups have signaled that there’s litigation strategies. There’s also the regulatory strategy. But, I think for us, one thing that is clear is that, whether it’s federally or locally, we actually need to hold these newly elected members of Congress accountable, so that they’re actually working to include trans people in their policies,” Chestnut said.

The losses have reminded activists of laws passed in the early 2000s to restrict same-sex couples from getting married.

“In the 1990s and 2000s, ballot measures were one of the main ways that the rights of LGBTQ+ people were used to divide people. But ballot measure outcomes, including losses, reflect a moment in time, not a permanent verdict on the future of rights or what’s possible. We believe that, ultimately, people value fairness and respect the diversity that makes our communities stronger,” Bond said.

articles.title: Samantha Hudson, Laura Weissmahr y María Barrier denuncian que Policía les roció con gas pimienta en plena manifestación: "A punto de ahogarme"
articles.standfirst: Las tres estuvieron en la movilización llevada a cabo en la Gran Vía de Madrid
articles.summary: Las tres estuvieron en la movilización llevada a cabo en la Gran Vía de Madrid
articles.body: Este miércoles, 11 de noviembre, está siendo en toda España un día marcado por la huelga general. Los piquetes y manifestantes por todo el territorio nacional están siendo protagonistas a lo largo de la jornada, impidiendo que algunos trabajadores sí que acudan a sus respectivos empleos. Sin embargo, en puntos como la Gran Vía de Madrid, hubo una manifestación multitudinaria en la que la tensión fue evidente, con presencia de agentes de la Policía para intentar poner orden. Entre esta multitud estuvieron Samantha Hudson, Laura Weissmahr y María Barrier, quienes denunciaron que los efectivos desplegados en el lugar les rociaron con gas pimienta. En declaraciones recogidas por La Séptima, Samantha Hudson, apuntó que estuvo “a punto” de ahogarse con el gas pimienta: “Estábamos en primera línea sin ejercer violencia y nos han empujado contra la acera”. Por otro lado, María Barrier también apuntó lo siguiente al respecto. “Estábamos en primera línea y nos han echado a Laura, a Samantha y a mí directamente el spray en los ojos, el oído y las vías respiratorias”. “El spray pimienta ya es una bestialidad, pero que te lo echen directamente en los ojos cuando los tienes abiertos…”, denunció la periodista. Todo tuvo lugar sobre las 14:00 horas, tras unas dos horas de protesta en la que miles de personas cortaron la circulación fluida en la Gran Vía de la capital de España. Más allá de la reclamación de los precios de la vivienda y el alto coste de la vida, también se sumaron profesores que estaban convocados en Callao. En este contexto, los agentes de la UIP de la Policía Nacional instaron a los congregados a abandonar el lugar y, ante su negativa, los empujaron y terminaron cargando sobre ellos, viviendo momentos de tensión como los que comentaron Samantha Hudson, Laura Weissmahr y María Barrier.
